children: is gaining serious traction inside government and defense, with its public-sector business now the company's fastest-growing industry business at scale and defense revenue expanding 80% year over year. The acceleration gives Salesforce a potentially important new growth engine as U.S. agencies increase spending on artificial intelligence, cloud software and automation.
The update comes one year after Salesforce launched Missionforce, its government-focused platform combining AI, data, applications and cloud infrastructure.
Salesforce said Missionforce now supports operations across more than 30 countries, 60 U.S. federal agencies, all 15 Cabinet departments, all 50 states and all six branches of the U.S. military.
One of the biggest opportunities is a 10-year U.S. Army contract carrying a $5.6 billion ceiling to expand Missionforce National Security across the Army and Department of War.
The Army Human Resources Command is also using the platform to provide AI-powered services to 9.2 million soldiers, veterans, civilian employees and military families.
Salesforce is seeing adoption beyond the Army.

The U.S. Air Force has deployed Missionforce to modernize operations supporting a vehicle fleet valued at $13.5 billion, while the Transportation Security Administration is using an AI agent called Ace to handle roughly 100,000 traveler conversations each month.
Salesforce said Ace resolves 96% of routine inquiries without requiring human escalation and has reduced consumer-interaction costs by more than 90%.
The company is also collaborating with OpenAI to bring advanced AI models and accelerated computing into Missionforce workloads and secure government environments.
The strongest part of the update is not simply the number of agencies using Missionforce, but the combination of rapid defense growth and large, long-duration government contracts.
That could give Salesforce a more durable revenue stream while creating another route to monetize its AI investments.

Investors should watch how quickly the $5.6 billion Army ceiling converts into actual revenue, whether defense growth remains near current levels and whether deployments such as TSA's Ace expand across other agencies.

The opportunity is substantial, but government procurement cycles are long and contract ceilings do not guarantee full spending. The key question is whether Missionforce becomes a meaningful contributor to Salesforce's overall growth rather than remaining a fast-growing but relatively small public-sector niche.

title: Salesforce Finds New Winner Inside Its AI Strategy
